findings.quote: Stars and galaxies are the largest objects in this topic.
findings.problem: This opening sentence is new in the split, and it is a general claim that fails against the lesson's own stars. The lesson calls a white dwarf 'a small, hot, faint star about as wide as Earth', and Jupiter, a planet in this topic, is about 11 times as wide as Earth. A neutron star is 'about $20$ km across', smaller than Ceres or many asteroids. The next sentence then makes size a naming clue ('ask what it is made of and how big it is'), so a student told about an Earth-sized or 20 km object would rule out a star and answer wrongly. Found by testing the general statement against the exceptions the lesson itself names, per the reader rules' Sol-audit addition.
findings.source: Checklist B01; reader-rules.md 'Added after the Sol audit'; NASA Imagine the Universe, Neutron Stars (about 20 km across), https://imagine.gsfc.nasa.gov/science/objects/neutron_stars1.html; NASA Science, Stars (white dwarfs about Earth-sized), https://science.nasa.gov/universe/stars/

findings.quote: This lesson sorts stars and galaxies by those clues.
findings.problem: The new opening paragraph has four sentences, over the one-to-three-sentence limit. Four-sentence paragraphs moved unchanged from the parent, where the finding was open after rounds 1 to 3, also start at 'A star shines because of', 'A red star is the coolest', 'A star many times the Sun's mass' and 'Galaxies have three common shapes'.
